s0.why: [1] calls it a fast-moving current of hot gas and volcanic matter that flows along the ground away from a volcano.

s1.why: [2] gives extremely high speeds and temperatures; [3] gives deadliest of all volcanic hazards and produced by certain explosive eruptions.

s2.why: [8] and [32] have gravity separating dense rock that sinks and flows along the ground, [33] has lighter ash rising, and [9] names the dense part flow and the light part surge.

f0.why: [13] derives pyroclast from Greek for 'fire' and 'broken in pieces'.

f1.why: [14] says flows that glow red in the dark are called nuee ardente, French for 'burning cloud'.

f2.why: [5] lists density of the current, volcanic output rate and slope gradient as what speed depends on.

f3.why: [12] says pyroclastic currents can be observed on other astronomical bodies such as the moon.

f4.why: [10] says pyroclastic density currents can, in certain cases, flow over water.

q1.why: [18] says much of the erupted mixture sinks to the ground because it is denser than the atmosphere.

q2.why: [3] names pyroclastic flows the deadliest hazard and [1] describes them as hot gas currents flowing along the ground, matching the ground-hugging option.

q3.why: [5] makes speed depend on density, output rate and slope gradient; with the first two held equal only slope differs, and steeper-is-faster is the plain reading for a downhill current, though [5] does not spell out the direction.

q4.why: [8] and [32] say denser rock is pulled by gravity and sinks to flow along the ground, while [33] has lighter ash rising.

q5.why: [10] says the currents can flow over water with denser constituents sinking into it; the island shoreline is just a setting.

q6.why: [13] gives pyr 'fire' and klastos 'broken in pieces' as the Greek roots.
